A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the direct method of estimating information is an asymptotically consistent estimator of the mutual information when the joint distribution is stationary and ergodic and the stimulus is stochastic.

mutual information is a time-averaged quantity, and the direct method estimates this time-averaged mutual information under the assumption that the joint distribution of the response and the stimulus is jointly stationary and ergodic, but it estimates the variability of the response when the stimulus is not stationary or non-stochastic.

The main takeaway from our work is that
, when the stimulus is non-stationary, the direct estimate of mutual information is not meaningful.

, when the stimulus is non-stationary, information estimates based on the direct method are not estimates of mutual information and are therefore not measures of the amount of information conveyed by the stimulus.
, in order to estimate mutual information, the response must be jointly stationary with the stimulus, and that, in general, the direct method is a poor estimate of mutual information.
